commit.message:
8392077: AArch64: Remove redundant FADD in floating-point add reductions on NEON

NEON non-strictly ordered floating-point reduction instruction rules are
updated to avoid materialising a redundant `fadd`, and additionally now
use an immediate operand instead of a register.

Vector API and auto-vectorisation share the AddReductionV node which has
to support the needs of both - it models a scalar value plus a vector
operand.  Since `reduceLanes()` has no scalar source the Vector API
intrinsic generates an identity scalar value which is passed as the
first input to AddReductionVF/VD.  Because addition with the identity
value is unnecessary when implementing a Vector API reduction, NEON
non-strict floating-point reductions no longer generate an extra
instruction.  Furthermore, the matcher has been updated to use
zero-constrained immediate operands to guarantee that the scalar value
is zero.

Update the predicate of `reduce_non_strict_order_add2D_neon` to restrict
it to 128-bit vectors, ensuring vectors wider than 128 bits select
`reduce_addD_sve` for correct code generation on all SVE-capable
systems.

Before:

faddp   v26.4s, v18.4s, v18.4s
faddp   s19, v26.2s
fadd    s19, s19, s17 // accum(s19) += s17(value 0.0)

After:

faddp   v26.4s, v18.4s, v18.4s
faddp   s19, v26.2s

Throughput benchmarks are split into 2 different types, based on the
reduction benchmarks in
test/micro/org/openjdk/bench/vm/compiler/VectorAlgorithmsImpl.java

1. A naive version which performs lane reductions inside the loop, e.g.
   vectorDoubleAddReduce_naive
2. 'reduction_after_loop' version which performs element-wise addition
   inside the loop, followed by a single reduceLanes after the loop,
   e.g.  vectorDoubleAddReduce_reduction_after_loop

Benchmarking has been conducted on Arm Neoverse N1, Neoverse V2, as well
as Arm Cortex-A725, Cortex-X925 CPUs.

Mode: thrpt
Units: ops/us
ObjectAlignmentInBytes: 64

Number is speed-up, higher number is better

| Benchmark            | Type   | Count | A725 | X925 | N1   | V2   |
| naive                | Double | 128   | 1.0  | 1.0  | 1.0  | 1.0  |
| naive                | Double | 512   | 1.0  | 1.0  | 1.0  | 1.0  |
| naive                | Double | 2048  | 1.0  | 1.0  | 1.0  | 1.0  |
| naive                | Double | 4096  | 1.0  | 1.01 | 1.0  | 1.0  |
| reduction_after_loop | Double | 128   | 1.02 | 1.02 | 1.03 | 1.01 |
| reduction_after_loop | Double | 512   | 1.0  | 0.99 | 1.0  | 1.0  |
| reduction_after_loop | Double | 2048  | 1.0  | 1.0  | 1.0  | 1.0  |
| reduction_after_loop | Double | 4096  | 1.0  | 1.0  | 1.0  | 1.0  |
| naive                | Float  | 128   | 1.02 | 1.01 | 1.21 | 1.0  |
| naive                | Float  | 512   | 1.02 | 1.0  | 1.16 | 1.0  |
| naive                | Float  | 2048  | 1.02 | 1.0  | 1.14 | 1.0  |
| naive                | Float  | 4096  | 1.06 | 1.01 | 1.14 | 1.0  |
| reduction_after_loop | Float  | 128   | 1.02 | 1.02 | 1.03 | 1.01 |
| reduction_after_loop | Float  | 512   | 1.01 | 1.01 | 1.0  | 1.01 |
| reduction_after_loop | Float  | 2048  | 1.0  | 1.0  | 1.0  | 1.0  |
| reduction_after_loop | Float  | 4096  | 1.0  | 1.0  | 1.0  | 1.0  |

Speed-up is observed on Neoverse N1 for the naive Float benchmark, as
well as a slight general improvement for low trip counts of
reduction_after_loop.

As well as, a latency benchmark which uses reduction results in
subsequent reductions, which forms a latency-sensitive instruction
sequence.

Mode: avgt
Units: ns/op
ObjectAlignmentInBytes: 64

Number is reduction in time, lower number is better

| Count | Type   | A725 | X925 | N1   | V2   |
